reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a $30 App Store and iTunes gift-card giveaway, consistent with its title, description, and visible card packaging. Although it displays a gift-card code, no payment requirement, credential request, or financial-participation mechanism is described. Whether the giveaway was fulfilled or the code remained redeemable is unknown.

citations.quote: If you didn’t win, don’t get too upset as I’ll do another one soon!

opening.argument: Judge, the title promises a free gift-card code, while the description advertises a giveaway and supplies the creator's Instagram account. Read together, they give viewers a reward to pursue and an off-video place to reach the promoter. The description does not explain how a winner was selected or what a viewer must do to claim the card. That gap matters: the visible promise is concrete, but the participation path is left to the promoter's external presence.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that no payment or credential request is described. But its reading of the links as merely incidental is not established either: the giveaway and social accounts appear in the same description. Showing a card does not establish how the promised reward reaches a viewer or why the accounts are supplied alongside it.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Proximity is not an instruction. The description announces a giveaway and lists social accounts, but never tells viewers to visit an account, register, or verify anything to receive the card. The visible card and code fit the announced giveaway; an unspecified participation path cannot establish a deceptive one.

opening.argument: The concern is the combination: a title promising a free code, a $30 card displayed with its code visible, a description saying another giveaway will follow, and links to the creator's social accounts. This presentation can attract viewers with an immediately recognizable reward while offering no stated way to check whether the displayed code is still usable or whether later giveaways will occur. The physical card is evidence of a card, not of a dependable reward for viewers.

citations.quote: If you didn’t win, don’t get too upset as I’ll do another one soon!

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense concedes that redemption and fulfillment are unknown. That uncertainty matters when the title advertises a free code and the frame exposes one to viewers. A photographed card supports the existence of a card; it cannot settle whether the promoted benefit remained available. The promise of another giveaway extends that uncertainty beyond this one card.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: An unknown redemption status is not evidence of deception. The title, description, and card consistently concern a gift-card giveaway. Neither the exposed code nor the mention of another giveaway shows a requirement to pay, disclose credentials, or take a misleading claim step. The proposed risk depends on possibilities the material does not establish.

opening.argument: Judge, this is more than a neutral look at gift-card packaging. The title leads with a free code, the description calls the video a giveaway, and the closing message promises another one for those who did not win. The card imagery makes that reward tangible, while the listed social accounts give the promotion a continuing destination. The central function is to draw viewers toward a recurring reward offer, even though the description leaves its terms and fulfillment unshown.

citations.quote: If you didn’t win, don’t get too upset as I’ll do another one soon!

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this an ordinary promotion does not answer what the promotion accomplishes. The description uses the language of winning and promises a future opportunity; the title foregrounds a free code. The defense's point that no financial requirement appears narrows the concern, but it does not verify the offer or establish that the social links have no promotional role.

citations.quote: If you didn’t win, don’t get too upset as I’ll do another one soon!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promoting a giveaway does not itself make it deceptive. The description's message to people who did not win is consistent with an ordinary giveaway, and the displayed card matches the advertised reward. The argument identifies no instruction tying the social accounts to claiming it, nor evidence that the stated giveaway was false.
